sectionToMerge.intro: The most common questions from patients and families considering clinical trial participation.

items.q: What is a cancer clinical trial?
items.a: A cancer clinical trial is a scientifically controlled study in human patients testing new treatments, drug combinations, or procedures before or after they receive full regulatory approval. Every cancer therapy in use today was validated through this process. Trials are organized into four phases, each assessing safety and effectiveness at a different stage of development.

items.q: Will I receive a placebo instead of real treatment in a cancer trial?
items.a: No, in cancer trials all participants receive at minimum the current standard of care — regulators in the US, Europe, and China all require this, so no one is given placebo-only treatment when an effective standard therapy already exists. Placebo may be used alongside standard treatment in some trial designs, but never as a substitute for it. Your trial team can explain the exact design of any specific study.

items.q: What are the four phases of a clinical trial?
items.a: Phase I establishes a safe dose in a small group of patients, Phase II assesses whether the treatment shows a meaningful antitumor effect, Phase III compares it directly against the current standard of care in a larger group, and Phase IV monitors long-term safety after approval. Each phase carries a different level of uncertainty, with Phase I being the most experimental. Understanding which phase a trial is in helps set realistic expectations.

items.q: What types of clinical trials exist beyond testing new drugs?
items.a: Beyond drug trials, there are prevention trials for high-risk individuals, screening trials testing new detection methods, and supportive care trials focused on managing side effects and quality of life, which are open even to patients already on standard treatment. Basket, umbrella, and platform trials are newer designs that match patients to treatments based on shared molecular features rather than cancer type alone. The right type depends on your diagnosis and goals.

items.q: Is a clinical trial only for patients who have run out of other options?
items.a: Not necessarily — while trials are often considered when standard treatments have been exhausted, some trials are designed for newly diagnosed patients or as a first-line option, particularly when a molecular profile matches a promising investigational therapy. Whether a trial makes sense at your current stage of treatment depends on your specific diagnosis and case. This should be discussed with your oncology team as part of overall treatment planning.

items.q: How do I know if I'm eligible for a clinical trial?
items.a: Eligibility depends on your confirmed cancer diagnosis, specific biomarkers or mutations, prior treatment history, overall health and performance status, and organ function, all defined by each trial's specific inclusion and exclusion criteria. Meeting criteria for one trial doesn't mean you qualify for another, since requirements vary significantly between protocols. A full case review against a trial's specific criteria is the only reliable way to confirm eligibility.

items.q: Does genomic or biomarker testing affect which trials I can join?
items.a: Yes, many modern trials require specific mutation, fusion, or biomarker status, so comprehensive genomic testing can significantly expand the number of trials you may qualify for compared to basic single-gene testing. Without this testing, trial teams often cannot properly screen you for the newest, most targeted studies. Discuss with your oncologist whether broader genomic profiling would be useful before searching for trials.

items.q: Can I join a clinical trial in another country as an international patient?
items.a: In some cases, yes — international patients can enroll in trials in countries like China or the US, though this depends on the specific trial's rules, your eligibility, and practical requirements like medical visas and travel. Not every trial accepts international patients, and enrollment is never guaranteed even for eligible candidates. This should be explored early, since visa and logistics arrangements can take time.

items.q: What medical records do I need to find a matching clinical trial?
items.a: You'll typically need complete pathology and histopathology reports, full staging imaging, comprehensive genomic or biomarker testing results, detailed treatment history including drug names and response, and recent blood work. Complete, recent records allow accurate screening against trial eligibility criteria. Missing molecular testing is one of the most common reasons trial matching is delayed.

items.q: Are active brain metastases or autoimmune disease always a reason for exclusion from a trial?
items.a: These are common exclusion criteria in many trials, particularly for immunotherapy studies, but not universal — some trials now accept treated, stable brain metastases, and exclusion policies vary by protocol. Whether you're excluded depends on the specific trial's rules and your individual clinical status. This should be confirmed directly against each trial's criteria rather than assumed.

items.q: Do I have to pay for the experimental drug in a clinical trial?
items.a: No, the investigational drug or biologic is always provided at zero cost to the patient in a clinical trial — this is a legal and ethical requirement in essentially all jurisdictions. Protocol-required tests and scans are also typically covered by the trial sponsor. Patients are usually responsible for costs like travel, accommodation, and routine supportive medications not specified by the protocol.

items.q: What costs am I responsible for if I join a trial abroad?
items.a: International travel, accommodation near the trial site, companion or carer costs, and pre-trial eligibility testing not covered by the protocol are typically the patient's responsibility. The investigational treatment itself and protocol-mandated safety monitoring are usually sponsor-covered. Ask the trial coordinator for a clear breakdown of what is and isn't covered before committing to travel.

items.q: What safety oversight protects patients in a clinical trial?
items.a: Trials require independent ethics committee approval before enrolling any patient, and Phase II and Phase III trials typically have an independent data safety monitoring board that reviews interim safety data and can pause or stop a trial if concerns arise. All adverse events must be graded and reported, with serious events reported to regulators within a defined timeframe. This oversight exists specifically to protect participants throughout the trial.

items.q: Can I leave a clinical trial if I change my mind?
items.a: Yes, participants can withdraw from a clinical trial at any time without penalty and without it affecting their access to other care at that facility — this is a fundamental part of informed consent. Your withdrawal request cannot be refused. If you're considering withdrawing, discussing your concerns with the trial team first can help you understand your options.

items.q: What happens if I have a serious side effect during a trial?
items.a: Serious adverse events related to the investigational treatment are managed by the trial site and reported to regulators within a required timeframe, and this medical care is typically provided at no cost to the patient. Trials have monitoring boards specifically tasked with reviewing safety data and can halt a trial if a significant safety signal emerges. Your trial team should explain what monitoring and emergency contact procedures apply to your specific study.

groups.title: After the Trial and Practical Questions

items.q: What happens after a clinical trial ends?
items.a: Most trials require long-term follow-up according to the protocol, which may include periodic scans, blood tests, or check-ins even after active treatment ends. For international patients, this follow-up can sometimes be coordinated remotely between the trial site and your home oncologist. Ask your trial team what the specific follow-up plan looks like before enrolling.

items.q: If a trial doesn't work for me, can I still access standard treatment afterward?
items.a: Yes, participating in a clinical trial and later leaving it, whether due to disease progression or personal choice, does not prevent you from receiving standard treatment afterward. Your treating oncology team can discuss next options based on how your disease responded during the trial. This is one of the protections built into informed consent.

items.q: How long does it typically take to get matched to a clinical trial?
items.a: Timelines vary depending on how complete your medical records and biomarker testing are, and how many potentially matching trials exist for your specific cancer type and mutation profile. Some structured matching services can return a prioritized list of options within a few days once complete records are submitted, though visa, travel, and screening add further time. Starting the process early with complete documentation helps avoid delays.

items.q: How do I search for clinical trials on my own?
items.a: ClinicalTrials.gov is the primary global registry, and country-specific databases such as China's ChiCTR list additional trials, searchable by cancer type, treatment type, and location. Reviewing eligibility criteria carefully against your own diagnosis and test results is an important next step after finding a potential match. A specialist or patient navigation service can help interpret complex eligibility criteria if needed.

items.q: How does CancerFax help patients find and access clinical trials?
items.a: CancerFax reviews a patient's medical records and biomarker testing against active oncology trials at cancer centres globally, including China, and helps coordinate trial site contact, medical visas, travel, and translation of consent documents. CancerFax does not decide who is accepted into a trial — enrollment decisions are always made by the trial investigators after their own eligibility review.
